title: Turning financial news into data you can test

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A headline lands, and within minutes it's mentioned in a thousand places. How do you turn that endless stream into something you can search, compare with market data, and test an idea on?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That sounds like drinking from a fire hose. Is that the job here?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It is. Antoine's project, AINewsTracker, is a FastAPI service that turns financial news into records you can search, analyze and line up with prices.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So what happens when a request comes in?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Picture an assembly line with four stations. A request reaches the news route and starts a collection job. The news service pulls the feed and creates article records. A metrics service reads the text. Then a repository stores the result in MongoDB.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right, and that's what keeps it tidy. Routes talk HTTP, models describe the data, services do the news work, and repositories keep database access in one place. Redis sits on top for caching.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What does a stored article actually hold?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Its URL, publication date and text, next to the analysis fields. The documentation links four kinds of records: a news source, its articles, comments on an article, and companies. A source carries language and country. A company's ticker ties mentions together, so different spellings of a name still point to one business.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The documented outputs are a sentiment label and score, detected tickers, a short summary and topic labels. Each answers a different question: which company is this about, what does it say, and how is it written.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. A strategy route hands backtest requests to a trading module. The labels become inputs to an experiment: pick a period, give the strategy the news that was available at that moment, and read what it reports back.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So the source stays attached the whole way.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's the neat part. A sentiment label traces back to its article and its publisher, and the date tells you when it was known. That makes every step easy to inspect.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So what should a listener take away?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That you can build a clean path from raw feed to historical experiment, with each piece doing one job. The full write-up has the architecture diagram, and every box in it links to its source file.
